div.head:
1788. Robert Southey to Grosvenor Charles Bedford, 27 June 1810Address: To/ G. C. Bedford Esqr/ Stafford Row/ Buckingham Gate/ London./ Single
Stamped: KESWICK/ 298
Postmark: E/ 30 JUN 30/ 1810
MS: Bodleian Library, MS Eng. Lett. c. 24. ALS; 3p.
Unpublished.
div.p: This evening there came a letter franked by that noble franker the first Lord,Spencer Perceval, Prime Minister and First Lord of the Treasury. – I opened it eagerly thinking to have certain tidings of your movements, & behold it contained nothing except a blank stamp, – not a receipt as usual, but a mere stamp, so that why it came, or what it is for, unless you can inform me I am likely never to know.

Will you contrive to have the sum of £3– 5s/ paid for me to Mr George Ridout George Ridout (1788–1871), later Lecturer and Vicar of Newland, Gloucestershire. in Paternoster Row, – his father is a surgeon I believe, John Gibbs Ridout (1758–1823), London apothecary. He had previously given medical advice to Coleridge. – but the Row is not very long, & is probably one of those places in which the inhabitants know who <are> their neighbours. I owe him this money for some books which he purchased for me in Spain, whither he went with Jacob the M.P. William Jacob (1761/2–1851; DNB), MP for Rye 1808–1812. He made a 6-month visit to Spain in 1809–1810 and published Travels in the South of Spain the following year. whom Whitbread The radical MP Samuel Whitbread (1764–1815; DNB). cross-examined in his character for of Council for Buonaparte.Edinburgh Annual Register, for 1808, 1.1 (1810), 432, reporting William Jacob’s speech in the Commons on 9 March 1808, retailing French atrocities at Puerto Real; Whitbread then rose to challenge Jacob and ask him if he had been an eye-witness to these scenes. & as I have no acquaintance with Ridout, & really feel much indebted to him for his xxx civility; I shall <be glad> to have the money part of the obligation settled as soon as convenient. You will not for a moment suppose that I am wishing you, an invalid, to perform this commission in any other way, than by sending him the money in a note, & requesting, if he be not at home when the messenger arrives, that he would acknowledge it by the twopenny post. Will you also let Miss Betham know that you are coming hither, – Colonel Peachy has left some little trinket for Edith in her hands, – as a memorial of his wife.
My cruel summer cold has taken up the quarters with me as usual, & my eyes & nose are suffering severely. I look anxiously for a line for you that I may secure your lodgings –
